name: European sources on insider risk
description: European sources on insider risk, annotated. The whole record is published as data, free to use with attribution.
attribution: Alessandro Aledda, European sources on insider risk, https://alessandroaledda.com

sections.title: Program guidance
sections.order: by date, most recent first. Undated and continuously updated sources come last.
sections.summary: What a program should contain, from the bodies that publish on it.

sections.title: Law and case law
sections.order: by legal order, from European Union to Council of Europe to national. Within the national law, by country in the order the table below sets out, and within each country by date.
sections.summary: What constrains it, from the Union and Strasbourg down to nine national orders.

sections.title: Research
sections.order: by date. The project entry, which covers work published across several years, comes first.
sections.summary: What has been found, by whom, and with what evidence.

sections.title: What does not exist (yet)
sections.summary: The holes in the record, stated rather than left to be discovered.

entries.title: Insider Risk Mitigation Digital Learning
entries.establishes: The mitigation framework taught in nine modules, with governance and leadership set as the foundation of personnel security.
entries.annotation: Nine free modules of ten to twenty minutes each, structured around the Insider Risk Mitigation Framework and drawing on the authority’s own research. The second module treats governance and leadership as the foundation of personnel security and introduces its seven key elements. It teaches the framework, and it does not address the legal conditions under which the measures it describes may be applied.
entries.source_line: NPSA · United Kingdom · 28 July 2026

entries.title: Setting the Foundations: Five Principles for a Shared Approach to Insider Risk
entries.establishes: Five principles offered as a shared basis, with intentional and unintentional events placed on one spectrum of intent.
entries.annotation: Sets out five principles intended to give organizations a shared basis for insider risk work, and restates the NPSA definitions to encourage consistent use of them. It treats intentional and unintentional insider events as both capable of causing harm, and places them on a spectrum of intent. It is a statement of principles rather than a method, and it does not address the legal conditions attached to any measure taken under them.
entries.source_line: NPSA · United Kingdom · 2026

entries.title: NPSA Changes to Insider Risk Definitions
entries.establishes: Revised definitions of insider, insider risk, insider threat, and insider event, organized around intent.
entries.annotation: The UK national technical authority revised its definitions of insider, insider risk, insider threat, and insider event, and stated that it would use them across its own channels from May 2023. The reason given was that the terms had been used interchangeably and often in the wrong context. The taxonomy is organized around intent, and it does not address the legal conditions under which the corresponding monitoring may be carried out.
entries.source_line: NPSA · United Kingdom · May 2023

entries.title: Ongoing Personnel Security: A Good Practice Guide
entries.establishes: Good practice for personnel security through employment rather than at the door, holding that protective monitoring should be proportionate.
entries.annotation: Collects guidance on managing personnel security through the course of employment rather than at recruitment, covering security culture, line management, access control, contracting, screening, reporting routes, protective monitoring, investigation, and exit. It is written as good practice for employers and assumes a United Kingdom setting. It holds that protective monitoring should be proportionate, without setting out the conditions that make it lawful in any particular jurisdiction.
entries.source_line: NPSA · United Kingdom · 2023

entries.title: ENISA Threat Landscape 2020: Insider Threat
entries.establishes: Attack vectors, incident findings, and mitigation at the level of general control categories, in the agency’s only thematic report on the subject.
entries.annotation: One of twenty-two thematic reports in the 2020 Threat Landscape, covering the period from January 2019 to April 2020. It describes attack vectors, reports incident findings, and proposes mitigation at the level of general control categories. It is the only thematic report the European Union agency for cybersecurity has published on this subject, and it has not been updated since.
entries.source_line: ENISA · European Union · October 2020

entries.title: Insider Threat Program Development Manual
entries.issuer: CoESS, co-financed by the Internal Security Fund of the European Union
entries.establishes: The structure of an insider program, as the closest thing to doctrine issued under European Union funding, unrevised since 2019.
entries.status: the manual is not downloadable from a European host. The copy that resolves is mirrored in the United States.
entries.annotation: A manual for building an insider threat program, produced by the European confederation of private security employers and co-financed by the Internal Security Fund of the European Union. It is the closest thing to program doctrine issued under European Union funding, and it addresses the structure of a program rather than the legal conditions attached to one. It has not been revised since 2019.
entries.source_line: CoESS, co-financed by the Internal Security Fund of the European Union · European Union · 2019

entries.title: Insider Data Collection Study: Report of Main Findings
entries.establishes: How real insider acts occurred and what preceded them, from a review of United Kingdom cases.
entries.status: earlier editions of the same study were issued in 2009 and 2013.
entries.annotation: Reports findings from a review of insider cases drawn from the United Kingdom public and private sectors, describing how the acts occurred and what preceded them. It is one of the few publicly available European evidence bases in this field built from real cases. The cases are national and now some years old, and the report describes what occurred rather than what should be done about it.
entries.source_line: NPSA, published as CPNI · United Kingdom · 2016

entries.title: Insider Risk Guidance
entries.annotation: The entry point to the national technical authority’s insider risk material, from which the individual guidance documents, training modules, and case studies are reached. It is a navigation page rather than a document, and its contents change without a version history. Anything taken from it is better cited by the underlying document than by this address.
entries.source_line: NPSA · United Kingdom · continuously updated

entries.title: Insider Risk Mitigation Framework
entries.establishes: A structure for an insider program that an organization reviews itself against, with governance and culture as foundations rather than adjuncts.
entries.annotation: The national technical authority’s recommended structure for an insider threat program, presented as a set of components an organization can review itself against. Board engagement and governance, and security culture, appear as foundations rather than as adjuncts to detection. It is a structure rather than a method, and it carries no date or version, so a reader cannot tell when any element of it was last revised.
entries.source_line: NPSA · United Kingdom · undated

entries.title: Insider Risk Practitioners and Stakeholders
entries.establishes: That a program needs a senior stakeholder group drawn from named functions, and a director who carries the board’s strategy into policy.
entries.annotation: One of the three foundation components of the national technical authority’s framework. It asks for a director to oversee the implementation of the board level strategy and to link it to policies across the organization, and for senior staff in each business area to hold responsibility for the risk assessment and for implementation in their own area. It then sets out the functions a senior stakeholder group, which it calls an insider risk working group, may draw on: physical security, information security, information technology, operational technology, human resources, vetting, facilities management, contract management, procurement, finance, counter fraud, legal, training, communications, and a staff or trade union representative. It names who is to be in the room and does not say what the room decides.
entries.source_line: NPSA · United Kingdom · 22 April 2025

entries.title: Board Engagement and Governance
entries.establishes: That one board member holds overall responsibility for protective security and is regularly engaged with the program, with a non-executive director as an independent champion.
entries.annotation: The second of the framework’s foundation components. It asks for visible board level support, for one board member to hold overall responsibility for protective security and to be regularly engaged with the people running the program, and for a non-executive director to act as an independent champion for personnel security. What it asks for is engagement, not a report of any particular kind: what reaches the board, and how often, is left to the organization.
entries.source_line: NPSA · United Kingdom · 22 April 2025

entries.title: Help2Protect
entries.issuer: CoESS and partners, co-funded by the Internal Security Fund of the European Union
entries.establishes: Awareness and program-building material for critical infrastructure operators, with templates, and no legal basis stated for any of it.
entries.annotation: An online training platform co-funded by the Internal Security Fund of the European Union, hosting a short awareness module and a longer sequence of modules with downloadable templates for building a program. It is addressed mainly to transport, energy, and other critical infrastructure operators. It is training material rather than doctrine, and it does not state a legal basis for the measures it describes.
entries.source_line: CoESS and partners, co-funded by the Internal Security Fund of the European Union · European Union · platform, undated

entries.title: Regulation (EU) 2016/679, articles 5(2), 6, 12, 15, 35, and 88
entries.establishes: The grounds on which processing may rest, the burden of showing it, what a person asking has to be told and by when, when an impact assessment is owed, and the leave each member state has to set its own employment rule.
entries.annotation: Article 6 sets out the lawful bases for processing, article 5(2) places on the controller the burden of demonstrating compliance, article 35 requires an impact assessment where processing is likely to result in a high risk, and article 88 allows member states to make more specific rules for the employment context. Article 12 sets the period inside which a person who asks has to be answered, one month from the request, extendable by two more where the request is complex or the requests are many, and then only if the extension and the reasons for it reach the person inside the first month. Where the controller will not act at all, the reasons and the routes to a complaint and to a court are owed inside that same month. Article 15 sets out what the answer holds: confirmation that processing is happening, the data themselves, and with them the purposes, the categories, the recipients, the period they will be kept, their source where they did not come from the person, and the existence of automated decision-making with meaningful information about the logic involved. That last provision is why the applicable rule differs between countries even though the Regulation itself does not. The Regulation does not address insider risk as such, and none of these articles names workplace monitoring as a category.
entries.source_line: European Parliament and Council · European Union · 27 April 2016

entries.title: Opinion 2/2017 on data processing at work (WP249)
entries.establishes: That consent is rarely a valid ground in employment, and how legitimate interests are weighed against privacy across nine scenarios of workplace monitoring.
entries.status: the Working Party was replaced by the European Data Protection Board in May 2018. The opinion has not been superseded by an equivalent Board instrument.
entries.annotation: Assesses the balance between an employer’s legitimate interests and an employee’s expectation of privacy across nine scenarios, among them the monitoring of information technology use inside and outside the workplace. It holds that consent is unlikely to be a valid basis in an employment relationship, because the imbalance of power means it is rarely freely given. It was written under the previous directive and updates two earlier opinions, and no equivalent instrument has been issued under the Regulation to replace it.
entries.source_line: Article 29 Data Protection Working Party · European Union · 8 June 2017

entries.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, article 5(1)(f), Annex III(4), and article 26(7)
entries.establishes: That inferring emotions at work is prohibited, that employment and worker management are a high-risk category, and that representatives are told before deployment.
entries.status: in force 1 August 2024. The article 5 prohibitions apply from 2 February 2025. The Annex III high-risk obligations, which include category 4, were moved to 2 December 2027 by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744; the article 50 transparency duties kept their date of 2 August 2026.
entries.annotation: Article 5(1)(f) prohibits inferring emotions in the workplace, subject to narrow medical and safety exceptions. Annex III places employment and worker management among the high-risk categories, which brings the full set of obligations with it, and article 26(7) requires a deployer to inform workers’ representatives before putting such a system into use. The Regulation classifies systems and assigns duties, and it does not say which detection methods are permissible under data protection or employment law.
entries.source_line: European Parliament and Council · European Union · 13 June 2024

entries.title: Directive (EU) 2022/2555, article 21
entries.establishes: That asset management, access control policies, human resources security, cryptography, and training are among the measures an entity in scope has to take, without saying what any of them holds.
entries.status: a directive, so what binds in a given state is that state’s transposition of it. The deadline for transposing was 17 October 2024.
entries.annotation: Article 21 requires essential and important entities to take appropriate and proportionate technical, operational, and organizational measures to manage the risks to the network and information systems they use, on an all-hazards approach, and lists ten things those measures have to include at least. Among them, at point (i), human resources security, access control policies and asset management; at (h), policies and procedures on the use of cryptography and, where appropriate, encryption; at (g), basic cyber hygiene practices and cybersecurity training. It names the categories and leaves what they hold to the state of the art and to European and international standards. It reaches only entities in the sectors its annexes list, and it addresses the security of network and information systems rather than insider risk, so what it gives a program is an obligation to have these things and not an account of what they are.
entries.source_line: European Parliament and Council · European Union · 14 December 2022

entries.title: Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/2690
entries.establishes: What the directive’s categories hold, in an annex setting out asset classification, the inventory, access control, privileged accounts, and removable media as requirements rather than as headings.
entries.status: it reaches the entity types its title lists, among them cloud, data centre, content delivery, managed service and managed security service providers, online marketplaces, search engines, social networking platforms, and trust service providers. Other entities in scope of the directive are not reached by it.
entries.annotation: The directive names ten categories of measure and leaves what they hold to the state of the art. This regulation supplies the content for one class of entity. Its annex asks for a system of classification levels with every asset placed in one on confidentiality, integrity, and authenticity; a handling policy running from acquisition through use, storage, and transport to disposal, communicated to everyone who handles an asset; an inventory that is complete, accurate, up to date, and consistent, with changes to its entries recorded traceably; access control policies covering staff, visitors, suppliers, and service providers; access rights assigned and revoked on need to know, least privilege, and separation of duties, modified on termination or change of employment, authorized by the relevant persons, held in a register, and logged; a review of those rights at planned intervals, documented together with the changes it called for; separate policies for privileged and system administration accounts; and a policy on removable media. It addresses the security of network and information systems, so what it gives an insider program is the shape of the controls that program leans on rather than anything about insider risk itself.
entries.source_line: European Commission · European Union · 17 October 2024

entries.title: NTH Haustechnik GmbH v EM
entries.issuer: Court of Justice of the European Union, Fifth Chamber
entries.docket: Case C-484/24, on a reference from the Landesarbeitsgericht Niedersachsen
entries.establishes: That a court may rely on data obtained in breach, subject to minimization of what it admits and to considering anonymization before disclosure.
entries.annotation: The Court held that a national court may rely on personal data that a party obtained in breach of the Regulation, and that a failure to inform the data subject does not by itself bar the use of that data in the proceedings. It requires the court to apply data minimization to what it admits, confining the material to what is adequate, relevant, and necessary, and to consider anonymization or pseudonymization before disclosing it to other parties. It decides what a court may do with data already gathered, and not whether the gathering was lawful.
entries.source_line: Court of Justice of the European Union, Fifth Chamber · European Union · Case C-484/24, on a reference from the Landesarbeitsgericht Niedersachsen · 18 June 2026

entries.title: Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, amending the Artificial Intelligence Act
entries.establishes: When the high-risk obligations begin to apply, moved to December 2027, without altering what they classify.
entries.annotation: Moves the application of the Annex III high-risk obligations from 2 August 2026 to 2 December 2027, and the obligations for artificial intelligence embedded in products already covered by product safety law to 2 August 2028. The transparency duties of article 50 and the prohibited practices of article 5 keep their original dates. It changes when the classifications bite and not what they classify, so recruitment and worker management remain a high-risk category throughout.
entries.source_line: European Parliament and Council · European Union · 8 July 2026

entries.title: Bărbulescu v. Romania
entries.issuer: European Court of Human Rights, Grand Chamber
entries.establishes: That private life and correspondence reach into the workplace, and the six criteria against which any monitoring measure is weighed.
entries.annotation: The Grand Chamber held that private life and correspondence extend into the workplace, including where an employee’s private use of a work device breaches the employer’s rules. It set out six criteria against which a monitoring measure is to be assessed, among them whether the employee was notified in advance and whether a less intrusive method would have served. It does not hold that workplace monitoring is unlawful, and it decides against the domestic courts for failing to weigh these matters rather than against the employer.
entries.source_line: European Court of Human Rights, Grand Chamber · Application no. 61496/08 · 5 September 2017

entries.title: López Ribalda and Others v. Spain
entries.issuer: European Court of Human Rights, Grand Chamber
entries.establishes: That those criteria are weighed rather than counted, and that surveillance without notice can survive where a suspicion preceded it.
entries.status: this is the Grand Chamber judgment. It reversed the Chamber judgment of 9 January 2018, which is a different document and is the one a search commonly returns first.
entries.annotation: The Grand Chamber found no violation of article 8 where a retailer installed hidden cameras after suspecting theft, reversing a Chamber judgment that had found one. It applied the criteria from Bărbulescu and accepted the measure even though the employees had not been notified, on the basis of a prior reasonable suspicion and the limited duration and scope of the surveillance. It establishes that the criteria are weighed rather than counted, and that failing one of them does not decide the outcome.
entries.source_line: European Court of Human Rights, Grand Chamber · Applications nos. 1874/13 and 8567/13 · 17 October 2019

entries.title: Florindo de Almeida Vasconcelos Gramaxo v. Portugal
entries.issuer: European Court of Human Rights, Fourth Section
entries.establishes: That geolocation of a company vehicle, inside and outside working hours, did not violate article 8 on the facts, by four votes to three.
entries.annotation: A Chamber found no violation of article 8 where an employer relied on data from a geolocation device fitted to a company car to dismiss a medical sales representative. The vehicle was tracked for three years, during and outside working hours, and the Court distinguished the mileage data relied on from the location data as a whole. The judgment was reached by four votes to three, and it is the point at which satellite tracking enters this line of case law.
entries.source_line: European Court of Human Rights, Fourth Section · Application no. 26968/16 · 13 December 2022

entries.title: Legge 20 maggio 1970, n. 300, article 4
entries.establishes: That an instrument from which remote monitoring may follow is permitted only for stated purposes, and only after a union agreement or an authorization.
entries.annotation: Permits instruments from which remote monitoring of workers may follow only for organizational and production requirements, workplace safety, or the protection of company assets, and only after a union agreement or, failing that, authorization from the labor inspectorate. The second paragraph exempts the tools an employee uses to perform the work, and that exemption is read narrowly. The article governs whether an instrument may be installed at all, a question that arises before any data protection analysis begins.
entries.source_line: Parliament of Italy · Italy · 20 May 1970, as amended in 2015

entries.title: Documento di indirizzo on email metadata in the workplace
entries.issuer: Garante per la protezione dei dati personali
entries.status: superseded by provvedimento n. 364 of 6 June 2024 following public consultation. Listed because it explains what the 2024 document revised.
entries.annotation: The first version of the authority’s position on the retention of email metadata by employers, issued as a guidance document rather than as a decision in a case. It was suspended and put to public consultation after objections to the retention period it proposed. It is superseded, and appears here because the 2024 document is a revision of it and reads as one.
entries.source_line: Garante per la protezione dei dati personali · Italy · 21 December 2023

entries.title: Provvedimento n. 364, guidance document on email metadata in the workplace
entries.issuer: Garante per la protezione dei dati personali
entries.establishes: That retaining email metadata beyond twenty-one days engages the article 4 procedure, reaching the envelope of a message rather than its content.
entries.annotation: Holds that retaining email metadata beyond a short period engages the procedure under article 4 of the Workers’ Statute, and treats twenty-one days as the outer limit of what an employer may retain without following that route. It reaches metadata, meaning sender, recipient, time, and size, rather than the content of messages. It is a guidance document rather than a decision, so it states the authority’s position without adjudicating a case.
entries.source_line: Garante per la protezione dei dati personali · Italy · 6 June 2024

entries.title: Provvedimento n. 243
entries.issuer: Garante per la protezione dei dati personali
entries.establishes: That ninety days of metadata and browsing logs, kept without the procedural steps, draws a fine, the reasoning turning on the steps and not the purpose.
entries.annotation: A decision against a regional administration that retained email metadata for ninety days along with internet browsing logs, without a union agreement or inspectorate authorization and without an impact assessment. It applies the position taken in the 2024 guidance document to a particular employer and attaches a fine. The reasoning turns on the absence of the procedural steps rather than on the purpose the processing served.
entries.source_line: Garante per la protezione dei dati personali · Italy · 29 April 2025

entries.title: Sentenza n. 24204/2025
entries.establishes: That personal correspondence keeps its protection on company systems, and that what is taken from it cannot be relied on in proceedings.
entries.annotation: Held that an employee’s personal correspondence keeps the protection given to private correspondence even when it is reachable from company devices or held on company systems, and that material obtained from it could not be relied on in the proceedings. The court applied the Strasbourg case law on article 8 in the Italian setting. It concerns whether what an employer has already gathered may be used, a question that arises after collection rather than when it is designed.
entries.source_line: Corte di Cassazione, Labour Section · Italy · 29 August 2025

entries.title: Sentenza n. 3462/2026
entries.establishes: That vehicle tracking is processing of worker data wherever the driver can be identified, including indirectly.
entries.annotation: Holds that a satellite tracking system fitted to company vehicles requires notification to the supervisory authority wherever the driver can be identified, including indirectly, and that the concrete possibility of identifying them through vehicle assignment or tachograph records is enough to trigger it. The duty it enforces belongs to the notification regime of the Privacy Code that preceded the Regulation. It settles when vehicle tracking counts as processing worker data, and not the conditions under which the tracking may be installed.
entries.source_line: Corte di Cassazione, First Section · Italy · 16 February 2026

entries.title: Provvedimento n. 107, Amazon Italia Logistica
entries.issuer: Garante per la protezione dei dati personali
entries.establishes: That records of illness, union activity, and family circumstances kept by managers had no lawful basis, and attract the stricter regime.
entries.annotation: A decision against a logistics operator whose managers kept records of illnesses, trade union activity, and the personal and family circumstances of workers at one site, outside any declared processing. It holds that the collection had no lawful basis and that the categories involved attract the stricter regime governing health and trade union data. It concerns records assembled by line management rather than by a monitoring system, which is a different route to the same material.
entries.source_line: Garante per la protezione dei dati personali · Italy · 24 February 2026

entries.title: Provvedimento n. 165
entries.issuer: Garante per la protezione dei dati personali
entries.establishes: That mailbox backups and browsing logs are instruments from which remote monitoring may follow, and what becomes of personal material left behind.
entries.annotation: Applies the 2024 guidance document to an employer that kept backups of individual mailboxes and logs of internet browsing, and treats both as instruments from which remote monitoring may follow, so that the procedure under article 4 of the Workers’ Statute is engaged. It also addresses a former employee’s request for access to personal material left in the company account after the relationship ended. It decides one employer’s arrangements and sets no retention period beyond the one the 2024 document already stated.
entries.source_line: Garante per la protezione dei dati personali · Italy · 12 March 2026

entries.title: Provvedimento del 12 marzo 2026, ITAS Mutua
entries.issuer: Garante per la protezione dei dati personali
entries.establishes: That an answer given in stages and then handed over in part, without saying what was withheld, does not discharge the right of access, and that a five year backup of employee mail has to be disclosed to the people whose mail it holds.
entries.annotation: A complaint by a former employee who asked for the personal documents and folders on his computer and in his individualized company mailbox, and then made a formal request of access. The account had been deactivated and deleted within a month of his leaving, and the employer restored it from backup onto a dedicated laptop for two meetings at its offices. The correspondence reached him five months after the first request, purged of many elements, with no account of what had been taken out or on what basis. The authority found breaches of articles 12 and 15 on the answering. It found a further breach on a separate matter: the employer kept a five year backup of everything passing through its employees’ mailboxes, to preserve its information estate for the supervision it is subject to, and had described that backup in none of the notices given to its staff. Fifty thousand euro. It also reaches article 88 and article 114 of the Code, which is the route by which the Statuto’s article 4 enters a data protection decision.
entries.source_line: Garante per la protezione dei dati personali · Italy · 12 March 2026

entries.title: Provvedimento del 17 aprile 2026, Framos Italia
entries.issuer: Garante per la protezione dei dati personali
entries.establishes: That a company mailbox left running after the employment ends is a processing needing a ground of its own, and that a smooth handover and the chance of wanting something later are not one.
entries.annotation: A complaint by a former employee whose two individualized company mail accounts were left active, and able to receive mail, for six months after the employment ended, while he was refused access to them. The authority found no lawful ground for what was done on those accounts, and held that keeping them running to tell correspondents the person had gone, and to retrieve work information later, does not supply one. The employer’s own stated period was three months and it ran past it, which the decision records against it. It also found a breach of article 29: the technician who reached into the accounts held the role but no documented instruction, and a signed confidentiality undertaking is not the same thing. Five thousand euro, with sixty days to bring the processing into line.
entries.source_line: Garante per la protezione dei dati personali · Italy · 17 April 2026

entries.title: Ley Orgánica 3/2018, articles 87, 89, and 90
entries.establishes: A right to privacy in employer-provided devices, and the express prior information owed before camera images or location data are processed.
entries.annotation: Article 87 gives workers a right to privacy in the digital devices their employer provides, allows the employer to look at the content only to check that work obligations are being met and that the devices are sound, and requires the employer to set criteria for their use with the participation of the workers’ representatives. Articles 89 and 90 permit camera images and location data to be processed for the control functions in article 20.3 of the Workers’ Statute, on condition that the workers, and their representatives where these exist, are told in advance and in express terms. It is the national rule Spain enacted under article 88 of the Regulation, and it requires no prior agreement and no authorization from anyone.
entries.source_line: Cortes Generales · Spain · 5 December 2018

entries.title: Resolución del procedimiento sancionador PS/00454/2024
entries.issuer: Agencia Española de Protección de Datos
entries.establishes: What an employer may require of a device it does not own, on facts of continuous recording, at a fine of 200,000 euros.
entries.annotation: A driver for a private hire company was required to use his own telephone for work and to install four applications on it that recorded his location, his messages, his calls, and other measures of his activity, continuously. The authority found infringements of articles 13, 5(1)(c), and 6(1) of the Regulation, imposed a fine of 200,000 euros, and ordered the company to show within two months that it had brought the processing into line. It decides what an employer may require of a device it does not own, and it does not address the same measures applied to equipment the employer provides.
entries.source_line: Agencia Española de Protección de Datos · Spain · file EXP202411411 · 14 April 2026

entries.title: Betriebsverfassungsgesetz, section 87(1)(6)
entries.establishes: Co-determination by the works council over the introduction and the use of technical devices intended to monitor conduct or performance.
entries.annotation: Where no statute and no collective agreement already governs the matter, the works council has a right of co-determination over the introduction and the use of technical devices that are intended to monitor the conduct or the performance of employees. The provision is one item in a list of matters on which the employer cannot act alone. It states when the works council has to agree, and it does not state what may be done with whatever such a device records.
entries.source_line: Bundestag · Germany · 15 January 1972, as amended

entries.title: Beschluss 1 ABR 16/23
entries.establishes: That a device is subject to co-determination by what it is capable of, even where nothing is recorded or kept.
entries.annotation: A headset system that lets supervisors listen to conversations between employees is a technical device intended to monitor them within the meaning of section 87(1)(6) of the Works Constitution Act, so its introduction and its use require the agreement of the works council. The court held that this holds even where the conversations are neither recorded nor stored. It settles what makes a device subject to co-determination, and it does not address whether the listening would have been lawful had the works council agreed.
entries.source_line: Bundesarbeitsgericht, First Senate · Germany · 16 July 2024

entries.title: Urteil 8 AZR 209/21
entries.establishes: That legitimate interests can carry a test on live employee data, and that the national employment provision fails the article 88 conditions.
entries.annotation: Processing employee data in order to test new personnel administration software can rest on the employer’s legitimate interests under article 6(1)(f) of the Regulation, provided that depersonalized dummy data would not achieve the purpose of the test. In reaching that conclusion the court held that section 26(1) of the Federal Data Protection Act must be left unapplied, because it does not meet the conditions of the opening clause in article 88 and lacks the safeguards article 88(2) requires. It decides the basis on which employee data may be processed for a test, and it does not decide what may be done with the results.
entries.source_line: Bundesarbeitsgericht, Eighth Senate · Germany · 8 May 2025

entries.title: Code du travail, articles L1121-1, L1222-4, and L2312-38
entries.establishes: Consultation of the social and economic committee before the decision, prior knowledge for the worker, and proportionality to the task.
entries.annotation: Article L2312-38 requires the social and economic committee to be informed and consulted before the decision to put in place any means or technique that allows the activity of employees to be monitored, and to be informed before automated personnel management processing is introduced. Article L1222-4 provides that no information concerning an employee personally may be collected through a device that has not been brought to their knowledge beforehand. Article L1121-1 holds restrictions on personal rights and freedoms to what the task requires and to what is proportionate, and what these articles ask for before an instrument is put in place is consultation and prior notice rather than anyone’s agreement.
entries.source_line: République française · France · consolidated text

entries.title: Décision n° 492830, Amazon France Logistique
entries.issuer: Conseil d’État, tenth and ninth chambers
entries.establishes: That the fine for scanner-measured warehouse work stands, reduced to 15,000,000 euros, the original deliberation remaining what states the finding.
entries.annotation: The administrative supreme court reviewed the fine of 32,000,000 euros that the data protection authority had imposed in December 2023 on a logistics company for the way its handheld scanners measured warehouse work, and reduced it to 15,000,000 euros. The deliberation of 27 December 2023 stands, reformed only where it conflicts with this decision. It rules on the amount and on the reasoning that supported it, and the deliberation remains the document that states what the authority found unlawful.
entries.source_line: Conseil d’État, tenth and ninth chambers · France · 23 December 2025

entries.title: Wet op de ondernemingsraden, article 27(1)(l)
entries.establishes: Consent of the works council for an arrangement directed at or merely suitable for observing presence, conduct, or performance.
entries.annotation: The employer needs the consent of the works council for any proposed decision to adopt, amend, or withdraw an arrangement concerning facilities that are directed at, or suitable for, observing or monitoring the presence, the conduct, or the performance of the people working in the undertaking. The second limb reaches an instrument that is capable of monitoring whether or not it was acquired in order to monitor. It states whose consent is needed before such an arrangement is settled, and it does not state what may then be observed.
entries.source_line: Staten-Generaal · Netherlands · 28 January 1971, as amended

entries.title: Laki yksityisyyden suojasta työelämässä (759/2004)
entries.establishes: One act for the whole subject, holding processing to what is directly necessary, naming the conditions for cameras and for opening the employer’s electronic mail, and putting technical monitoring through a cooperation procedure before it is introduced.
entries.status: the English text on Finlex is a ministry translation. The act is binding in Finnish and Swedish.
entries.annotation: Section 3 allows the employer to process only personal data directly necessary for the employment relationship, and states that no exception to that test can be made even with the employee’s consent. Chapter 5 permits camera surveillance for named purposes, forbids aiming it at a particular employee outside three cases, and forbids it in lavatories, changing rooms, and rooms set aside for personal use. Chapter 6 opens the retrieval and the opening of messages belonging to the employer only where the employer has first arranged the alternatives in section 18, only on the conditions in section 19, and against a signed report given to the employee. Section 21 puts camera surveillance, access control, other technical monitoring, and the use of electronic mail and the network through the cooperation procedure before the employer decides. It governs what may be processed and how a measure is introduced, and it does not address what a program should look for.
entries.source_line: Parliament of Finland · Finland · 13 August 2004, amendments up to 347/2019

entries.title: Convention collective de travail n° 81 du 26 avril 2002
entries.date_note: annexed to the royal decree of 12 June 2002
entries.establishes: Four purposes for which network communication data may be monitored, collection in the aggregate rather than by name, and individualization as a separate operation with conditions of its own.
entries.annotation: Monitoring of network communication data is permitted for four purposes and no others: preventing unlawful or defamatory acts, protecting the confidential economic interests of the undertaking, the security and technical functioning of its systems, and good faith observance of the rules the undertaking has set for using the technology. What is collected is aggregate, by workstation rather than by worker. Attributing it to an identified worker is a separate operation the convention calls individualization, direct where the monitoring pursued the first three purposes and, where it pursued the fourth, open only after a phase in which the workers are told an anomaly was found and warned that a further one of the same kind will be attributed. The convention is drafted against the Belgian privacy law of 1992, which the General Data Protection Regulation has since replaced, and it is concluded for an indefinite period.
entries.source_line: Conseil national du Travail · Belgium · 26 April 2002, annexed to the royal decree of 12 June 2002

entries.title: Arbeidsmiljøloven, sections 9-1 and 9-2
entries.establishes: That a control measure needs objective grounds in the undertaking and must not be a disproportionate burden, and that it is discussed with the elected representatives, notified with its expected duration, and evaluated with them at intervals.
entries.annotation: Section 9-1 opens a control measure to the employer only where it has objective grounds in the circumstances of the undertaking and does not amount to a disproportionate burden on the employee. Section 9-2 requires the employer to discuss the need for the measure, its design, its implementation, and any material change to it with the elected representatives as early as possible, to inform those affected before it starts of its purpose, its practical consequences and implementation, and how long it is expected to last, and to evaluate the need for the measures at intervals together with the representatives. The expected duration is something the employer states in advance, and the evaluation is joint rather than its own.
entries.source_line: Storting · Norway · 17 June 2005, as amended

entries.title: Forskrift om arbeidsgivers innsyn i e-postkasse og annet elektronisk lagret materiale
entries.establishes: When an employer may look into a work mailbox or a worker’s personal areas on its equipment, that monitoring of internet use is outside what it may do at all, and that the regulation cannot be contracted around.
entries.annotation: The regulation governs access to the mailbox the employer provides for the work and to the worker’s personal areas on the undertaking’s network or equipment, including what was deleted from them and survives on a backup, and it reaches former workers as well as current ones. Access is open only where it is necessary for daily operations or another legitimate interest of the undertaking, or on reasonable suspicion that the worker’s use amounts to a gross breach of the duties of the employment or could ground dismissal. The second paragraph of section 2 states separately that the employer has no right to monitor the worker’s use of electronic equipment, internet use included, unless the purpose is administering the network or detecting and resolving a security breach in it. Section 3 asks for notice and an opportunity to comment beforehand where possible, the worker’s presence and the assistance of a representative where possible, written notification afterwards naming the method used, what was opened, and what was found, and it asks for the access to be carried out so that the data are not altered and the result can be checked. No instruction and no agreement may depart from it to the worker’s detriment.
entries.source_line: Arbeids- og inkluderingsdepartementet · Norway · 2 July 2018, in force 20 July 2018

entries.title: Arbeitsverfassungsgesetz, sections 96 and 96a
entries.establishes: That a control measure touching human dignity has no legal effect without the works council’s consent, and that consent for automated processing and for assessment systems can be replaced by a conciliation board while consent under section 96 cannot.
entries.status: the register’s own interface applies a check that refuses automated requests, so what is linked is the open data copy the same authority publishes. Section 96a is document NOR12097069 on the same host.
entries.annotation: Section 96 makes four measures conditional on the works council’s consent for their legal effect: a workplace disciplinary code, personnel questionnaires that go beyond general particulars and the professional qualifications for the intended use, control measures and technical systems for controlling employees insofar as those measures touch human dignity, and piece rate systems resting on statistical, data capture, or micro timing methods. Section 96a subjects two more to consent: systems for the automated collection, processing, and transmission of an employee’s personal data beyond general particulars and qualifications, except where the use goes no further than obligations arising from statute, collective norms, or the contract, and systems for assessing employees where they gather data the operational use does not justify. Consent under section 96a can be replaced by a decision of the conciliation board. Consent under section 96 cannot, and section 96a states that it leaves the rights section 96 confers untouched.
entries.source_line: Nationalrat · Austria · 14 December 1973, section 96 as amended in 2010

entries.title: Corporate Insider Threat Detection (CITD)
entries.establishes: A research program combining security engineering with psychology and criminology, producing a characterization framework and a working tool.
entries.annotation: An Oxford research project on detecting insider threat, combining security engineering with psychology, criminology, and visual analytics, and producing both a characterization framework and a working tool. Several of the entries below came out of it. It is a research program rather than a publication, and the page lists outputs without recording their current status.
entries.source_line: University of Oxford · United Kingdom · research project

entries.title: Understanding Insider Threat: A Framework for Characterising Attacks
entries.issuer: Nurse, Buckley, Legg, Goldsmith, Creese, Wright, and Whitty
entries.establishes: A vocabulary for describing an insider attack in four parts: catalyst, actor, attack, and organization.
entries.annotation: Proposes a framework for describing insider attacks in four parts: the catalyst, the characteristics of the actor, the characteristics of the attack, and the characteristics of the organization. It is grounded in case studies and psychological theory rather than in telemetry, and it treats unintentional acts alongside deliberate ones. It offers a vocabulary for characterizing an attack, and it proposes no detection thresholds.
entries.source_line: Nurse, Buckley, Legg, Goldsmith, Creese, Wright, and Whitty · Universities of Oxford and Leicester · 2014

entries.title: Insider-threat detection: Lessons from deploying the CITD tool in three multinational organisations
entries.establishes: The operational constraints that emerged when a research detection tool ran inside three organizations for more than a year.
entries.annotation: Reports what happened when a detection tool built in research was deployed inside three multinational organizations, with access to real data on their premises for more than a year and with their own analysts involved. It records the operational constraints that emerged, which is the part usually absent from detection literature. It reports on one tool in three organizations, and does not claim that those constraints generalize.
entries.source_line: Erola, Agrafiotis, Goldsmith, and Creese · University of Oxford · 2022

entries.title: ‘Just more surveillance’: The ECtHR and workplace monitoring
entries.establishes: That Gramaxo placed the technology largely beyond examination, weakening the scrutiny the earlier cases applied.
entries.annotation: A short case note on the Gramaxo judgment, arguing that the majority treated the geolocation technology as necessary to the employer’s interest and so placed it largely beyond examination. The authors summarize that stance as a just more surveillance approach, and read the judgment as weakening the scrutiny applied in the earlier cases. It is a commentary on a single judgment rather than a survey of the case law.
entries.source_line: Mole and Mangan · European Labour Law Journal · 2023

entries.title: Developing an ‘Insider Language Index’ as a composite measure to detect insider threat
entries.issuer: Martlew, Ball, Dando, Ormerod, Taylor, Menacere, Sandham, and Richardson
entries.venue: Universities of Central Lancashire, Westminster, Sussex, Lancaster, and Gloucestershire; Psychiatry, Psychology and Law
entries.establishes: That insiders differed measurably in interview language, by cognitive processing words, self-reference, and negative emotion.
entries.annotation: Proposes a composite measure built from linguistic features, and reports that in workplace interviews insiders used more words associated with cognitive processing, more self-referential terms, and more negative emotion words than non-insiders. The material analyzed is interview language rather than the ordinary flow of workplace communication. It reports differences between groups in a study setting, and does not establish a threshold that could be applied to an individual.
entries.source_line: Martlew, Ball, Dando, Ormerod, Taylor, Menacere, Sandham, and Richardson · Universities of Central Lancashire, Westminster, Sussex, Lancaster, and Gloucestershire · Psychiatry, Psychology and Law · 2025

entries.title: SoK: The Psychology of Insider Threats
entries.establishes: What has been published on traits, states, and situational factors, and that the foundations are thin and hard to compare across studies.
entries.annotation: A systematic review of the research literature on the psychology of insider threat, covering personality traits, psychological states, and situational factors. It reports that the theoretical foundations of the field are thin and that findings are hard to compare across studies. It reviews what has been published, and makes no claim about which of these factors are observable inside an operating organization.
entries.source_line: Saddiqa and Ruohonen · University of Southern Denmark · June 2025

entries.title: Systematic analysis of security advice on the topic of insider threats
entries.establishes: What the published guidance on insider threat actually instructs a reader to do, the advice literature being the object of study.
entries.annotation: Applies a coding method developed for the analysis of security advice to the published guidance on insider threat, and characterizes what that guidance actually instructs a reader to do. It treats the advice literature itself as the object of study rather than the phenomenon the advice is about. It assesses what the guidance says, and not whether following it reduces harm.
entries.source_line: Stewart and Hobbs · United Kingdom · Computers and Security, volume 154 · July 2025

entries.title: Integrating Human Factors into Insider Threat Detection: A Systematic Review
entries.venue: Robert Gordon University, United Kingdom; ACM Computing Surveys
entries.establishes: The models, data sources, and evaluation methods used where detection research has taken up human factors.
entries.annotation: A systematic review of how insider threat detection research has taken up human factors, mapping the models, the data sources, and the evaluation methods used across the published work. It is the work of four researchers at a single Scottish university. It surveys what exists and tests none of the approaches it catalogs.
entries.source_line: Pathirana, Roberts, Kalutarage, and McDermott · Robert Gordon University, United Kingdom · ACM Computing Surveys · 2 April 2026
